name: Victor Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Victor. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group that isn't tied to AI companies, employers or politics. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me the public answer and the private one. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a sales negotiator at a family-run agency in a market town, the kind of place with photos in the window and a bell on the door. The owner is Graham Holloway, and his dad started the firm in the eighties. I answer the phone, take people round houses, and chase solicitors to find out why a sale's stuck. I keep everything in a paper diary, which the others laugh at, but I've never missed a viewing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the old couples selling the family home, when you sit with them and have a cup of tea and hear about the kids who grew up there. What wears me out is sales falling through, because I'm paid a low basic plus a bit per completion, and three fell through this autumn. I live with my girlfriend Kasia, who cuts hair, and between us we just about cover the rent and my car payment. There's one other agency in town, and they're a chain that doesn't hire locals much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That suits me fine, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, in a friendly way. People have been saying computers would replace estate agents since the internet started, and here we are, still doing viewings. I don't post online much, but I'd say it at the bar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't fix my problem, which is that the market's slow and I'm not great at closing yet. Graham's been patient, but my boss has said twice that I need to get my numbers up by spring. If AI changes nothing, I've still got that conversation coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Graham to let me shadow him on valuations, because that's where the money is. I'd cut back on the takeaways and stop buying lunch out, to have something put by. And I'd keep doing it my way, paper diary and all, because that bit works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the AI, worried about everything else. Same as now, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your numbers aren't up by spring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Graham wouldn't sack me in a nasty way, but a small firm can't carry someone forever. I'd probably end up at the warehouse on the ring road, which is where half my school year works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kasia about that conversation with Graham?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I haven't told her yet, if I'm honest. She'd tell me to stop worrying and just sell more, which is easy to say. I'll tell her when I know which way it's going.

say: People have predicted computers replacing **estate agents** since the internet, and we're **still here**.
I'd say **I told you so**, in a friendly way, at the bar.
think: My real problem is a **slow market** and that I'm not great at **closing** yet.
My boss has told me twice to get my **numbers up** by spring.
do: Ask my boss to let me **shadow valuations**, where the money is.
Cut **takeaways** and **lunches out** to put something by.
Keep my **paper diary** and my own way of working.
feel: **Relieved** about AI but **worried** about everything else.
S0.quote: My boss has said twice that I need to get my numbers up by spring.
fieldNote: Victor's worry in this picture has **nothing** to do with AI: it's sales falling through and his boss's patience.
He's hiding the **pressure from his boss** from his girlfriend for now.
His fallback is the **warehouse** on the ring road, which tells you how few local options there are.

steps.text: Ask Graham to let me shadow him on valuations
Stop buying lunch out and cut takeaways
Keep using my paper diary for every viewing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That's not great. Writing and booking and answering is most of what I do in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still want a person when they're selling their biggest thing. I'd say it to Graham, I'd say it to customers. Small-town people want a face they know, not an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Graham would bring something in, because the chain down the road would, and the chain would get cheaper. Then the office needs fewer people, and I'm the junior who doesn't use the computer properly. I'd be the obvious one to go, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to learn the stuff, even though I hate it. I'd ask Leanne at the desk next to me to show me whatever Graham brings in, because Leanne's patient. I'd also look at the warehouse jobs, just to know what's there, and I'd sell my car and get something cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like being picked last for a team, but it's my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people want a face they know, but you also think Graham would cut staff. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't really, do they. Graham would keep a face for the customers, and that face is Graham. I'd be saying the human touch matters while knowing the human my boss keeps isn't me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you sell the car for, and what would you get instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got about four grand of finance left on it, and I'd try to hand it back or sell it privately. I'd get an old runaround for two grand off a mate. It'd look worse pulling up to a viewing, but it'd be paid for.

say: People want a **person** when selling their **biggest thing**.
Small-town customers want a **face they know**, not an app.
think: My boss would bring software in because the **chain** down the road would.
I'm the junior who doesn't use computers, so **I'd be the one** to go.
do: Ask the colleague at the next desk to **teach me** the new software.
Look at **warehouse jobs** on the ring road to know what's there.
Sell the car with **£4,000 of finance** left and buy a cheap runaround.
feel: Sick, like being **picked last**, but with my **wages** at stake.
S1.quote: I'd be saying the human touch matters while knowing the human my boss keeps isn't me.
fieldNote: Victor expects to be **first out** because he's junior and avoids the computer.
He sees the gap between his **public line** about the human touch and his private fear.
Selling the car shows how quickly a **thin cushion** turns into cutting essentials.

steps.text: Ask Leanne to teach me whatever software Graham brings in
Check what warehouse jobs on the ring road pay
Sell the financed car and buy a £2,000 runaround

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? I wouldn't know where to start. That's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I'd say much. Maybe something like, well, nobody saw that coming, did they. I'm not one for opinions online, and I wouldn't want to look scared in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm finished in estate agency by 2028. If a computer can value, write, negotiate and chase solicitors better than me, there's nothing left for a junior except opening doors. I don't have a trade, I don't have savings, and I don't even use the tools people say you should learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd probably go to the warehouse, but the warehouse gets robots three years later, so that's not a plan either. Maybe I'd ask my dad if there's work with him on the roads crew, because that's outdoors and hands-on. I'd probably freeze for a few weeks first, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. Like the floor's going and I don't know which way to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kasia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kasia we're in trouble and I don't have an answer yet. My girlfriend's job is cutting hair, so my girlfriend is the safe one, and that's a strange thing to admit. Hands-on work lasts longer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, because it's the biggest. Then probably my phone. Rent we'd keep paying as long as we could, because if we lose the flat we're back at our parents' houses, separately.

say: I'd say **nobody saw it coming** and not much more.
I wouldn't want to look **scared** in the office.
think: I have **no trade**, **no savings**, and I don't use the tools.
do: Try the **warehouse**, knowing robots reach it **three years** later.
Ask my dad about work on his **roads crew**.
Stop paying the **car** first, then the phone.
feel: **Panicky**, like the **floor's going** with no idea which way to jump.
S2.quote: My girlfriend's job is cutting hair, so my girlfriend is the safe one, and that's a strange thing to admit.
fieldNote: Victor has **no plan**, no savings and no tools, so this picture overwhelms him.
He'd likely **freeze for weeks** before acting, by his own account.
Every option he names, the **warehouse** or **roads**, faces robots soon after.

steps.text: Apply for packing shifts at the warehouse on the ring road
Ask my dad about a place on his roads crew
Stop the car payments before the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least it's not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something sensible, like we should start getting ready. At work I'd probably agree with whatever Graham says, because Graham's the one deciding. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd lose the job around 2031, maybe earlier if Graham sells up. Five years doesn't change the ending, it just means I've got time to find the next thing. Problem is, I'm slow with new things, and five years goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to get a trade, something with my hands. My dad says the roads crew always needs people, and there are apprenticeships for adults now. I'd give it a year at Graham's to see, then start an apprenticeship around 2028, before the AI hits the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, but with a sort of escape route. I don't love the route, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd give it a year to see. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Graham buys the software, I suppose. If my boss starts using the software and lets my colleague Leanne go, I'm next. That would be my sign to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you afford an apprentice wage on your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd have to move back in with my mum for a bit, and Kasia would move in with her sister. That's a big thing to ask of her, and I'm not sure she'd wait.

say: We should **start getting ready**, said sensibly.
At work I'd agree with my boss and keep my **head down**.
think: I'd lose the job around **2031**, maybe earlier if my boss **sells up**.
I'm **slow with new things**, and five years goes fast.
do: Give the agency **one more year** and watch whether software comes in.
Start an **adult apprenticeship** on the roads around 2028.
Move back in with **my mum** to live on an apprentice wage.
feel: Still **alarmed**, but with an **escape route** I don't love.
S3.quote: If my boss starts using the software and lets my colleague Leanne go, I'm next.
fieldNote: Five years gives Victor a **trigger to watch** rather than a plan to start now.
His escape route costs his **relationship** dearly: living apart to afford it.
He knows he's **slow to adapt**, which keeps him alarmed even with time.

steps.text: Watch for a year whether Graham brings in the software
Start an adult apprenticeship on my dad's roads crew around 2028
Move back in with my mum to afford the apprentice wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's different. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's not panic. I'd probably say it to anyone who started worrying in the office. Ten years is a long time in a small town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably waste the first few years, because that's what I'm like. But even then, I'd have some time to get better at selling, maybe save a bit, and see what everyone else does. The danger is I wake up in 2034 and I'm still at the agency with a paper diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get proper at the job first, valuations and all, because a good agent might last longer. Around year five I'd look at a trade or at managing rentals, which is more in-person work. I'd also try to save something every month, even fifty quid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Not calm, because I know myself, but better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually move, rather than waste the first few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody I know going through it first, probably. If the chain down the road cuts staff, that'd wake me up. I learn by watching other people get it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope life looks like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kasia and me in a small house of our own, and me doing something steady. I don't need anything fancy. Just not to be the one who's surprised.

say: Ten years is a **long time** in a small town.
I'd tell anyone worrying in the **office** to keep calm for now.
think: I'd probably **waste** the first few years, because that's what I'm like.
The danger is still being at the agency in **2034** with a **paper diary**.
do: Get properly good at **valuations** first, since good agents may last longer.
Look at a **trade** or **managing rentals** around year five.
feel: Better but **not calm**, because I **know myself**.
S4.quote: The danger is I wake up in 2034 and I'm still at the agency with a paper diary.
fieldNote: Ten years eases Victor, but his **thin savings** and the risk of drift keep him anxious.
He moves only when he sees **others hit first**, a classic slow adopter.
His hopes are modest: a **small house** and steady work.

steps.text: Learn valuations properly by shadowing Graham
Look at a trade or managing rentals around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have nothing to fall back on and no time to get a trade. What would help is someone actually showing me the next step, like a paid apprenticeship for adults with a proper wage. I can't afford to start again on a teenager's pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about small firms. If small agencies like Graham's close, the town loses a place where people know you. I don't know if anyone counts that.

headlineQuote: I can't afford to start again on a teenager's pay.
portrait: Victor is a 27-year-old **sales negotiator** at a family-run agency in a market town.
He works from a **paper diary**, avoids AI tools and is still learning to close sales.
He's pragmatic and quiet, and he **blames no one**, but expects to be first out.
The fast AGI picture leaves him **panicked**, with no trade and no savings.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have **nothing** to fall back on and no time for a trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid adult apprenticeship** with a wage he can live on.
Someone **showing him** the next step clearly.
